topic_title: Top 15 Dog Breeds That Make the Best Road Trip Buddies
intro: A good travel dog settles in the back seat, stays quiet in a motel room and greets strangers at rest stops calmly. That depends more on temperament and barking than on size. Energy matters in a specific way: a high-energy dog can be a great hiking partner at the destination, but it needs real exercise at every stop or it becomes restless after hours of driving. Also weigh crate space, how it copes with heat in a parked car, and whether it gets along with the cats and dogs it will meet along the way.

picks.description: The Cavalier is the easiest travel companion on this list. At 13 to 18 pounds it rides comfortably in a crate on the back seat, and it is rated low for barking, so motel corridors and campground neighbors are rarely disturbed. It is gentle with children, cats and other dogs, which matters at rest stops, dog-friendly patios and relatives' homes. Its exercise needs are moderate, around 30 to 45 minutes a day, so a few short walks during a long driving day keep it content. Cavaliers want to be with their people, which suits trips where the dog goes everywhere. The trade-offs: the silky coat picks up burrs and needs brushing every few days, and the breed is prone to heart problems, so pack its medical records.
picks.best_for: Travelers wanting a calm, quiet dog that fits easily in a crate
picks.quirky_fact: Cavaliers were bred as lap warmers for English nobility, so long stretches of sitting with their people suit them.
picks.skip_if: You plan long, strenuous hikes or must leave the dog alone in rooms

picks.description: The Whippet is a medium sighthound of 25 to 40 pounds that is quiet, gentle and good with children and other dogs, and it is rated good with cats, though many still chase small animals outdoors. Its energy is moderate in a particular way: it loves a short, fast sprint in a secure area, then sleeps for hours, which fits a day of driving well. It is rated low for barking and has a short coat that sheds little and needs only a quick wipe, so it leaves little mess in a car or hotel room. The drawbacks are its thin coat and low body fat, so it needs a jacket in cold weather and soft bedding in the car, and it should stay leashed at stops because it can bolt after wildlife.
picks.best_for: Travelers wanting a clean, quiet medium dog that naps between stops
picks.quirky_fact: Whippets can reach about 35 miles per hour, yet most spend the rest of the day curled up asleep.
picks.skip_if: You want to let your dog run off-leash at trailheads

picks.description: The Greyhound is a large dog, usually 60 to 70 pounds, but it travels more like a calm medium dog. It is rated low for barking, gentle with children and other dogs, easy to train, and content with moderate exercise of two or three walks a day plus an occasional sprint in a fenced area. Many retired racing Greyhounds are already used to being transported, crated and handled. The short coat sheds little and needs only a weekly brush. Size is the main limit: a Greyhound needs an SUV, wagon or hatchback cargo area, and a few motels have weight limits. It feels cold easily and should not ride on hard surfaces without padding. Some Greyhounds have a strong chase instinct, so test cat tolerance individually and keep it leashed outside.
picks.best_for: Owners with a roomy car wanting a large but calm travel dog
picks.quirky_fact: Greyhounds are often nicknamed '45-mile-per-hour couch potatoes' because they sleep much of the day.
picks.skip_if: You drive a compact car or stay where weight limits apply

picks.description: The Boston Terrier is compact at 12 to 25 pounds, easy to train and friendly with children, cats and other dogs, so it handles the mix of strangers and new animals that comes with travel. Its short coat sheds lightly and needs almost no grooming on the road. Around 30 to 45 minutes of exercise a day is enough, so a couple of brisk walks at rest stops cover it. Barking is moderate, and some Bostons alert at unfamiliar noises in hotel rooms. The main concern is heat: the short muzzle makes Bostons prone to overheating, so travel in summer needs air conditioning, shaded stops, and planning so the dog is never left in a parked car. They also snore, which matters in a shared room.
picks.best_for: Travelers wanting a small, sociable, low-maintenance companion
picks.quirky_fact: The Boston Terrier is the official state dog of Massachusetts.
picks.skip_if: You are road-tripping through hot regions without reliable air conditioning

picks.description: The Miniature Schnauzer weighs 11 to 20 pounds, fits easily in a small crate, and is easy to train and good with children, cats and other dogs. Its energy is moderate, around 45 minutes a day, and it is curious enough to enjoy exploring new towns and trails without needing hours of running. The wiry coat sheds very little, which keeps car seats and rental furniture cleaner, but the beard collects water and food, so pack a towel. Barking is moderate and Minis are alert watchdogs, so expect some barking at hallway noises until the dog settles; practicing a quiet cue before the trip helps. The breed copes reasonably with cold and moderate heat, but like any dog should not be left in a parked car.
picks.best_for: Travelers wanting a small, sturdy, low-shedding dog for town and trail
picks.quirky_fact: Miniature Schnauzers were developed in Germany in the late 1800s as farm ratters and guard dogs.
picks.skip_if: You stay in thin-walled lodging and have not trained a quiet cue

picks.description: The Papillon is the lightest dog in this list at 5 to 10 pounds, small enough for a soft carrier on the back seat or in a hotel room, yet energetic and eager to explore. It is one of the easiest toy breeds to train and is good with children, cats and other dogs. Energy is high for its size, so it needs active breaks such as brisk walks or fetch in a quiet area, and it can manage short hikes. The silky single coat sheds little and needs brushing a couple of times a week. Barking is moderate, and Papillons are alert to new sounds. Their fine bones make them vulnerable to falls from car seats and to rough handling, so a secured carrier is safer than riding loose.
picks.best_for: Travelers wanting a tiny but active dog for short hikes
picks.quirky_fact: Papillons were favorites of European royalty and appear in many Renaissance paintings.
picks.skip_if: You travel with rough young children or want a sleepy lap dog

picks.description: The Brittany is a medium sporting dog of 30 to 40 pounds that is easy to train and friendly with children, cats and other dogs, so it handles campgrounds and busy rest areas well. Its energy is high: it needs an hour or more of running or hiking a day, which makes it a strong choice for trips built around trails, beaches and outdoor time, but a poor fit for long days of city driving. Plan for longer stops where it can run in a safe area. The medium, wavy coat sheds moderately and needs little grooming beyond a weekly brush and a check for burrs and ticks after hikes. Barking is moderate. Brittanys are sensitive and do best with a calm routine on the road.
picks.best_for: Hikers and campers wanting a mid-sized, trainable outdoor dog
picks.quirky_fact: The Brittany is named after the Brittany region of northwestern France, where it was developed as a bird dog.
picks.skip_if: Your trips are mostly driving, cities or long hotel stays

picks.description: The Toller is the smallest retriever, weighing 35 to 50 pounds, and fits in a medium crate in most hatchbacks and SUVs. It is easy to train and good with children, cats and other dogs. Energy is high, and Tollers love water, so trips that include lakes, rivers or beaches suit them; plan on at least an hour of activity a day. The medium-length, water-resistant double coat sheds moderately and needs weekly brushing, with heavier shedding seasonally, so bring a seat cover. Barking is moderate, but many Tollers make a loud, high-pitched excited noise known as the Toller scream, often when they anticipate getting out of the car, which can be surprising in campgrounds.
picks.best_for: Outdoor travelers heading to lakes, rivers and beaches
picks.quirky_fact: Tollers were bred to play along the shoreline to lure curious ducks within range of hunters.
picks.skip_if: You want a quiet dog for hotels or mostly urban trips

picks.description: The English Springer Spaniel is a medium sporting dog of 40 to 50 pounds that is friendly, easy to train and good with children, cats and other dogs. Its energy is high: it needs an hour or more of exercise daily, and it enjoys hiking, swimming and fetch, so it suits active trips with plenty of outdoor time. The medium, wavy coat sheds moderately, collects burrs and needs brushing two or three times a week, plus regular ear checks, especially after swimming, since the long ears are prone to infections. Barking is moderate. Springers are very people-oriented and dislike being left alone in an unfamiliar room, so plan activities where the dog can come along.
picks.best_for: Active families wanting an all-day outdoor travel companion
picks.quirky_fact: The name comes from the breed's original job of springing, or flushing, game birds from cover.
picks.skip_if: You will often leave the dog alone in hotel rooms

picks.description: The Australian Shepherd is a medium herding dog of 40 to 65 pounds that is easy to train, loyal, and good with children, cats and other dogs. Its energy is high, and its mind needs work as much as its legs: without a long run, hike or training session each day, it can become restless and pushy in a car or room. On an outdoor trip with daily hikes, though, it is an eager, capable partner. The medium double coat sheds moderately year round and heavily twice a year, so it needs weekly brushing and a seat cover. Barking is moderate. Aussies can be reserved with strangers and may try to herd children or other pets at busy stops, so steady handling helps.
picks.best_for: Experienced owners planning active, trail-focused road trips
picks.quirky_fact: Despite the name, the Australian Shepherd was developed mainly on ranches in the western United States.
picks.skip_if: Your trips involve long driving days with little outdoor activity

picks.description: The Vizsla is a lean, athletic large dog of 45 to 65 pounds with a short coat that sheds little and needs almost no grooming. It is easy to train, affectionate, and good with children and other dogs, but it is not rated as good with cats, which matters when staying with relatives or in shared rentals. Energy is high: it needs over an hour of vigorous exercise a day and suits running, biking and hiking trips. Vizslas are known as Velcro dogs and want to be with their people constantly, so they handle long drives well when you are in the car but struggle alone in a strange room. The thin coat gives little protection from cold, so pack a jacket for chilly mornings.
picks.best_for: Runners and hikers wanting a clean, affectionate athletic dog
picks.quirky_fact: The Vizsla is a Hungarian breed, and its rust-gold coat is one of its defining features.
picks.skip_if: You travel with or stay among cats, or must leave it alone

picks.description: The German Shorthaired Pointer is a large, versatile sporting dog of 45 to 70 pounds that is easy to train and good with children, cats and other dogs. Its short, dense coat sheds moderately but needs only a weekly brush, and it dries quickly after swimming. The challenge is energy: a GSP needs well over an hour of hard exercise daily, and on driving days it can become restless and vocal without long, active stops. It fits best on trips centered on trails, lakes and open country rather than city sightseeing. It needs a cargo area or large crate, and its strong hunting drive means wildlife at rest stops can pull its attention, so keep it leashed.
picks.best_for: Very active travelers planning outdoor trips with daily exercise
picks.quirky_fact: German Shorthaired Pointers have webbed feet, which help them swim strongly when retrieving.
picks.skip_if: You want a dog that naps through long highway days

picks.description: The Flat-Coated Retriever is a cheerful large dog of 60 to 70 pounds that is easy to train and good with children, cats and other dogs, so it is friendly with everyone at campgrounds and rest areas. Its energy is high and its playfulness lasts well into adulthood, so it needs an hour or more of exercise a day and enjoys swimming and fetch. The medium, straight coat sheds moderately and needs brushing a couple of times a week; a seat cover and towels help after swims. Barking is moderate. It ranks lower here because of its size in the car and its shorter lifespan of about 8 to 10 years, with a notable cancer risk in the breed.
picks.best_for: Families with a large vehicle wanting a playful water-loving dog
picks.quirky_fact: Flat-Coated Retrievers are nicknamed the Peter Pan of dogs because they stay puppyish for years.
picks.skip_if: You have a small car or want a calm, settled dog

picks.description: The Weimaraner is a large, athletic dog of 55 to 90 pounds that is easy to train and good with children and other dogs, but it is not rated as good with cats, and its prey drive is strong. It needs well over an hour of vigorous exercise a day; without it, it can become anxious and destructive, especially when left alone in an unfamiliar room. The short, smooth coat sheds moderately and needs little grooming, which helps on the road. Barking is moderate. A Weimaraner suits travelers whose trips center on long runs or hikes and who keep the dog with them, and it needs a large vehicle and crate. Separation anxiety is common, so practice short absences before traveling.
picks.best_for: Very active owners who keep their dog with them all day
picks.quirky_fact: Weimaraners are nicknamed the gray ghost for their silvery coat and light eyes.
picks.skip_if: You have cats, a small car, or will leave it alone in rooms

picks.description: The Pointer is a large, lean sporting dog of 45 to 75 pounds that is easy to train and good with children, cats and other dogs. Its short, smooth coat sheds moderately and needs only a weekly brush, so it stays clean on long trips. Energy is high: Pointers were bred to cover ground all day, so they need long runs or hikes and can become restless in the car without them. Their thin coat makes them sensitive to cold, and their size means a cargo area or large crate. Barking is moderate. They suit outdoor trips with plenty of open space rather than city stops, and their strong hunting instinct means a leash at all times near wildlife.
picks.best_for: Outdoor travelers wanting a clean, athletic and friendly large dog
picks.quirky_fact: Pointers freeze and point with their nose toward hidden game, a behavior that appears even in young puppies.
picks.skip_if: Your trips are mainly long drives with short city stops

faqs.question: What size dog is best for road trips?
faqs.answer: Small and medium dogs are easiest because they fit in a crate on the back seat and are welcome in more motels. Large dogs can travel well too, especially calm ones like the Greyhound, but they need a cargo area or a large crate, and some pet-friendly hotels set weight limits. Check those limits along your route before you book.

faqs.question: How often should I stop with a dog on a road trip?
faqs.answer: A common guideline is a short stop every two to three hours for water, a bathroom break and a brief walk. High-energy breeds such as Australian Shepherds, Vizslas and Pointers need longer, more active breaks, such as a 20-minute walk or a game of fetch, to stay settled in the car. Always use a leash at rest stops, even with a reliable dog.

faqs.question: How should a dog ride in the car?
faqs.answer: A secured crate or a crash-tested harness clipped to the seat belt system is safer than letting a dog ride loose or on a lap. Keep dogs out of the front seat because of airbags, and do not let them ride with their heads out of the window. Never leave a dog in a parked car on a warm day, even with the windows cracked.

faqs.question: Which breeds are quietest on trips?
faqs.answer: In this list, the Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, Whippet and Greyhound are rated low for barking, which helps in motel rooms, campgrounds and shared rentals. The other breeds are rated medium and may bark at unfamiliar noises in new places. Bringing a familiar bed or crate cover and keeping a routine helps any dog settle at night.

faqs.question: How do I get a dog used to long drives?
faqs.answer: Start with short drives that end somewhere pleasant, like a park, and gradually lengthen them over a few weeks. Feed a light meal a few hours before leaving to reduce car sickness, keep the car cool, and bring the dog's usual bed or crate. If a dog drools heavily, pants or vomits in the car, ask a vet about motion sickness options.

seo_title: Best Dog Breeds for Road Trips and Car Travel (2026)
answer: The Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, Whippet and Greyhound are the best road trip dogs here: calm between stops, quiet in motels and campgrounds, and friendly with strangers and other pets. The deciding factor is how well a dog settles in the car and in new places, not how much stamina it has for the hike at the end.
method: We filtered a 150-breed dataset for breeds that are good with children and other dogs and easy or moderate to train, then ordered them by barking level, energy, size and how well each gets along with cats, putting calm, quiet and adaptable breeds first.
author: Elena Marsh
